reference.source: Blumgart's Surgery of the Liver, Biliary Tract and Pancreas
clinicalPearls: Sump syndrome is a late complication of side-to-side choledochoduodenostomy in which the segment of common bile duct distal to the anastomosis becomes a poorly drained blind pouch, or sump, that accumulates food debris, biliary sludge, and stones
The stagnant distal duct collects material that cannot clear through the papilla, leading to recurrent cholangitis, biliary obstruction, pain, and occasionally pancreatitis or hepatic abscess

It is chiefly of historical and residual relevance because side-to-side choledochoduodenostomy is now performed less often, having been largely superseded by Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy and endoscopic therapy
Symptoms may appear months to years after the original biliary bypass, so a history of previous biliary-enteric anastomosis is a crucial diagnostic clue
ERCP is the mainstay of both diagnosis and treatment, allowing sphincterotomy and clearance of debris and stones from the distal duct sump
Cross-sectional imaging and MRCP demonstrate the anastomosis, the distal ductal reservoir, and any pneumobilia, stones, or abscess
Pneumobilia is expected after a biliary-enteric anastomosis and should not by itself be interpreted as infection or gas-forming pathology
Refractory or recurrent disease may require surgical revision, typically conversion to a Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy with closure of the distal duct
reference.pathophysiology: A side-to-side choledochoduodenostomy joins the common bile duct to the duodenum above the papilla, leaving the segment of duct between the anastomosis and the sphincter of Oddi as a dependent cul-de-sac. Because bile preferentially drains through the more proximal, wider anastomosis, this distal segment is no longer flushed by normal bile flow and loses its physiological clearance. Reflux of enteric contents introduces food particles, vegetable matter, and bacteria into the poorly emptying pouch, where stasis promotes accumulation of debris and biliary sludge, precipitation of stones, and bacterial overgrowth. The trapped material intermittently obstructs the papilla or the anastomosis and provokes recurrent ascending cholangitis; persistent stasis and infection can extend to cause pancreatitis when the pancreatic orifice is involved, or seed hepatic abscesses. The clinical picture therefore reflects chronic stagnation and infection within an anatomically dependent, non-draining distal duct rather than a primary stone or stricture elsewhere.
additionalDifferentials: Cholangitis from another cause of biliary obstruction
Ascending cholangitis related to sphincter of Oddi dysfunction
Pancreatitis of biliary or other aetiology
additionalInvestigations: Liver biochemistry showing a cholestatic pattern during symptomatic episodes
Blood cultures and inflammatory markers when cholangitis is suspected
Abdominal ultrasound to assess the biliary tree and detect stones or abscess
MRCP to delineate the anastomosis, the distal duct sump, and any retained debris or stones
Contrast-enhanced CT to identify complications such as hepatic abscess or pancreatitis
ERCP for direct visualisation, sump clearance, and therapeutic sphincterotomy
redFlags: Acute cholangitis with fever, rigors, jaundice, and haemodynamic compromise
Development of hepatic abscess or persistent sepsis despite antibiotics
Progressive jaundice suggesting anastomotic stricture or fixed obstruction
Recurrent severe episodes indicating need for surgical revision
reference.prognosis: Endoscopic sphincterotomy with clearance of the sump is effective in most patients and relieves recurrent cholangitis, giving a good outlook; recurrent or refractory disease that requires surgical conversion to a Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy also generally does well once the dependent distal segment is eliminated.
pitfalls: Failing to elicit the history of a previous side-to-side choledochoduodenostomy and so missing the diagnosis
Misinterpreting expected post-anastomotic pneumobilia as evidence of infection or gas-forming disease
Attributing recurrent cholangitis to simple retained stones without recognising the underlying sump anatomy
Overlooking a hepatic abscess or pancreatitis as a complication of chronic biliary stasis
Persisting with repeated endoscopic clearance when definitive surgical revision is warranted
references: Blumgart's Surgery of the Liver, Biliary Tract and Pancreas
Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Perform ERCP with endoscopic sphincterotomy and clearance of retained debris and stones from the distal duct sump as the mainstay of treatment
Treat episodes of ascending cholangitis promptly with broad-spectrum antibiotics covering enteric organisms alongside biliary drainage
Drain any complicating hepatic abscess and manage associated pancreatitis supportively
Reserve surgical conversion to a Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy for recurrent or endoscopically refractory disease
Monitor liver biochemistry and inflammatory markers during symptomatic episodes and surveil for recurrence
Refer to hepatobiliary surgery and gastroenterology for combined endoscopic and surgical planning
